        "text": "#!/bin/sh\n# chr-launch.sh: run the OFFICIAL mikrotik/chr image (MikroTik RouterOS Cloud\n# Hosted Router) as a containerlab node, image untouched.\n#\n# The image is MikroTik's own Docker Hub distribution (Alpine + qemu +\n# /diskimage/chr-<ver>.img + /start.sh). This script is bind-mounted into the\n# node and set as its entrypoint by the containerlab `mikrotik_chr` kind. It replaces\n# the image's /start.sh, which is not orchestration-ready (containerlab#3116):\n# it scans interfaces once before containerlab attaches the links, bridges the\n# management NIC so the container IP never reaches the router, and imports no\n# startup config.\n#\n# What it does (vrnetlab's mikrotik/routeros launch.py is the model, re-done\n# with the image's own busybox + qemu: no python, no ftp client, no tc):\n#   1. waits for the CLAB_INTFS data interfaces containerlab attaches (eth1..N)\n#   2. management, transparent: the container's eth0 is bridged with the VM's\n#      ether1 tap, and eth0's addresses and default gateways move into RouterOS\n#      ether1. The router IS the node's management address: every service and\n#      LLDP reach it directly, nothing is port-forwarded. The image ships only\n#      busybox (no tc), so this uses a bridge where vrnetlab uses tc-mirred\n#   3. data: one tap per container interface, bridged pairwise (ethN <-> tapN,\n#      LLDP forwarded). NIC order in the VM follows the eth index, so container\n#      ethN is always RouterOS ether(N+1), even with gaps\n#   4. after boot, over IPv6 link-local on the management bridge (no address is\n#      added to the management network): sets the credentials and the identity,\n#      configures ether1 with the management addresses and keeps their return\n#      path in its own VRF (`mgmt`, below), then fetches\n#      /ftpboot/config.auto.rsc (the containerlab startup-config, when present)\n#      from the launcher and `/import`s it\n#   5. prints the ready marker on the container log and waits on qemu\n#\n# Restart (docker restart, containerlab restart --node): RouterOS keys an\n# ethernet interface on its MAC. A NIC that comes back with a new MAC is a NEW\n# device (ether1 becomes ether3) and the DHCP client bound to ether1 never\n# binds. Docker re-rolls the container's eth0 MAC whenever the netns is\n# recreated, so the node id that seeds every NIC MAC and the data NIC count are\n# persisted in the container on the first boot and reused: the restarted qemu\n# carries the same NICs in the same order and RouterOS keeps ether1..N and\n# their config. The REST bootstrap is skipped on a restart; the management\n# step re-runs and re-applies the container's current addressing.\n#\n# Architectures: the image's own qemu (qemu-system-x86_64 on amd64,\n#   qemu-system-aarch64 + edk2 on arm64), KVM when /dev/kvm exists, else TCG.\n# Args (the kind's Cmd): --hostname H [--username U --password P]\n#   (unknown flags are ignored); credentials default to the USERNAME/PASSWORD env\n# Env (all optional, set under the node's `env:`); MEM, CPUS and DISK are the\n#   official image's own variables:\n#   MEM (qemu -m value, default 256 MiB + 8 MiB per data NIC and vCPU), CPUS (default 1),\n#   DISK (default 128M), CHR_INTF_WAIT (s, 60), CHR_BOOT_WAIT (s, 300)\n# Serial console: port 5000 inside the container\n#   (docker exec -it <node> nc 127.0.0.1 5000); the container itself has no\n#   address on the management network.\n# Ready: /.chr-launch-ready exists once RouterOS is ready (the kind's default\n#   healthcheck); it is removed at every start.\n# Log lines (docker logs clab-<lab>-<node>), all prefixed \"chr-launch:\":\n#   \"RouterOS ready\"                   login + startup config done\n#   \"startup config import FAILED: …\"  the router rejected the .rsc (RouterOS's\n#                                      own reason, with the line number)\n#   \"credential bootstrap FAILED: …\"   the user/password step failed\n#   \"management setup FAILED: …\"       the ether1 address / mgmt VRF step failed\n#\n# Copyright 2026 NetPilot Labs\n# Licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License.\n# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause\n\nset -u\n\n# Credentials come from the USERNAME/PASSWORD env the kind sets (no quoting\n# limits on the password); --username/--password still override them.\nUSERNAME=\"${USERNAME:-admin}\"\nPASSWORD=\"${PASSWORD-admin}\"\nHOSTNAME_ARG=\"\"\nwhile [ $# -gt 0 ]; do\n    case \"$1\" in\n        --username) USERNAME=\"$2\"; shift 2 ;;\n        --password) PASSWORD=\"$2\"; shift 2 ;;\n        --hostname) HOSTNAME_ARG=\"$2\"; shift 2 ;;\n        --connection-mode) shift 2 ;;\n        --trace) shift ;;\n        *) shift ;;\n    esac\ndone\n[ -n \"$HOSTNAME_ARG\" ] || HOSTNAME_ARG=\"$(hostname)\"\n\nCPUS=\"${CPUS:-1}\"\nDISK=\"${DISK:-128M}\"\nINTF_WAIT=\"${CHR_INTF_WAIT:-60}\"\nBOOT_WAIT=\"${CHR_BOOT_WAIT:-300}\"\nINTFS=\"${CLAB_INTFS:-0}\"\nSTARTUP_CFG=/ftpboot/config.auto.rsc\n# Per-container state in the rw layer: survives every restart, gone with the\n# container (destroy, redeploy --cleanup).\nDONE_MARKER=/.chr-launch-bootstrapped\nREADY_FILE=/.chr-launch-ready\nID_FILE=/.chr-launch-node-id\nNICS_FILE=/.chr-launch-nics\nMGMT_TABLE=mgmt\n# every management object the launcher creates carries this comment, so each\n# boot can find and re-apply them, and SaveConfig can leave them out\nMGMT_COMMENT=clab-mgmt\nMGMT_BR=br0\n# eth0's addressing as last seen: a launcher re-run in the same network\n# namespace finds eth0 already bridged and bare\nMGMT_FILE=/.chr-launch-mgmt\nSYSNET=/sys/class/net\n\nlog() { echo \"chr-launch: $*\"; }\nrm -f \"$READY_FILE\"\n\nFETCH_PORT=8080\n\n# ---- disk -----------------------------------------------------------------\nIMG=\"\"\nfor f in /diskimage/*.img; do [ -f \"$f\" ] && IMG=\"$f\" && break; done\nif [ -z \"$IMG\" ]; then\n    log \"no /diskimage/*.img in this image: not a RouterOS CHR image\"\n    exit 1\nfi\n# Only GROW the disk to the floor: an image already larger keeps its tail.\ndisk_bytes() {\n    case \"$1\" in\n        *G|*g) echo $(( ${1%[Gg]} * 1024 * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;\n        *M|*m) echo $(( ${1%[Mm]} * 1024 * 1024 )) ;;\n        *K|*k) echo $(( ${1%[Kk]} * 1024 )) ;;\n        *) echo \"$1\" ;;\n    esac\n}\nwant_bytes=\"$(disk_bytes \"$DISK\")\"\ncur_bytes=\"$(stat -c %s \"$IMG\" 2>/dev/null || wc -c < \"$IMG\")\"\nif [ \"$cur_bytes\" -lt \"$want_bytes\" ] 2>/dev/null; then\n    truncate -s \"$DISK\" \"$IMG\"\nfi\n\n# ---- wait for containerlab's data interfaces ------------------------------\n# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # interface names are ethN, ls is safe here\ncount_intfs() { ls -d \"$SYSNET\"/eth[1-9]* 2>/dev/null | wc -l; }\nwaited=0\nwhile [ \"$(count_intfs)\" -lt \"$INTFS\" ] && [ \"$waited\" -lt \"$INTF_WAIT\" ]; do\n    sleep 1\n    waited=$((waited + 1))\ndone\nlog \"interfaces: $(count_intfs) of $INTFS expected after ${waited}s\"\n\n# ---- qemu command line ----------------------------------------------------\n# The image's own qemu and firmware, as its /start.sh selects them.\ncase \"$(uname -m)\" in\n    aarch64|arm64)\n        QEMU=\"qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -pflash /usr/share/qemu/edk2-aarch64-code.fd\"\n        TCG_CPU=\"-cpu cortex-a57\" ;;\n    *)\n        QEMU=\"qemu-system-x86_64\"\n        TCG_CPU=\"\" ;;\nesac\nif [ -e /dev/kvm ]; then\n    ACCEL=\"-cpu host -accel kvm\"\nelse\n    ACCEL=\"$TCG_CPU -accel tcg,split-wx=on\"\n    log \"no /dev/kvm: running under TCG emulation (slow boot)\"\nfi\n\n# MACs: unique per node AND per NIC. The container's eth0 MAC is unique per\n# node, so its LAST TWO octets identify the node; the NIC's last byte is the\n# interface index (00 = mgmt, 01 = ether2, …). Two nodes sharing a NIC MAC on\n# a link drop each other's frames as their own. The id is read on the FIRST\n# boot only and persisted (see Restart in the header).\nnode_id=\"$(cat \"$ID_FILE\" 2>/dev/null)\"\ncase \"$node_id\" in\n    [0-9a-f][0-9a-f]:[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]) ;;\n    *)\n        e=\"$(cat \"$SYSNET/eth0/address\" 2>/dev/null)\"\n        if [ -n \"$e\" ]; then\n            o2=\"${e##*:}\"; rest_mac=\"${e%:*}\"; o1=\"${rest_mac##*:}\"\n            node_id=\"$o1:$o2\"\n        else\n            node_id=\"$(hexdump -n2 -e '2/1 \"%02x:\"' /dev/urandom | sed 's/:$//')\"\n        fi\n        printf '%s\\n' \"$node_id\" > \"$ID_FILE\" 2>/dev/null \\\n            || log \"node id $node_id not persisted: a restart will renumber the NICs\"\n        ;;\nesac\nNET=\"-netdev tap,id=mgmt,ifname=tap0,script=no,downscript=no -device virtio-net,netdev=mgmt,mac=52:54:00:$node_id:00\"\n\n# ---- management: eth0 + tap0 on one bridge, eth0's addressing to the VM ----\nip_global() { # ip_global <4|6> <dev>: the first global address/prefix\n    ip -\"$1\" addr show dev \"$2\" 2>/dev/null \\\n        | sed -n '/scope global/s/^ *inet6\\{0,1\\} \\([^ ]*\\) .*/\\1/p' | head -n1\n}\nip_gw() { # ip_gw <4|6>: the default gateway\n    ip -\"$1\" route show default 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^default via \\([^ ]*\\) .*/\\1/p' | head -n1\n}\nM4=\"$(ip_global 4 eth0)\"; M6=\"$(ip_global 6 eth0)\"\nG4=\"$(ip_gw 4)\"; G6=\"$(ip_gw 6)\"\nif [ -n \"$M4$M6\" ]; then\n    printf 'M4=%s\\nM6=%s\\nG4=%s\\nG6=%s\\n' \"$M4\" \"$M6\" \"$G4\" \"$G6\" > \"$MGMT_FILE\" 2>/dev/null || true\nelif [ -f \"$MGMT_FILE\" ]; then\n    # shellcheck disable=SC1090  # written by this script, four plain assignments\n    . \"$MGMT_FILE\"\nfi\nlog \"management: ${M4:-no IPv4}${M6:+, $M6} via ${G4:-no gateway}${G6:+, $G6}\"\n\ntunctl -t tap0 >/dev/null 2>&1 || ip tuntap add dev tap0 mode tap\nif [ ! -e \"$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR\" ]; then\n    _mtu=\"$(cat \"$SYSNET/eth0/mtu\" 2>/dev/null || echo 1500)\"\n    ip addr flush dev eth0\n    # The launcher's side of the bootstrap channel: IPv6 link-local on the\n    # bridge only. eth0 and tap0 are plain bridge ports.\n    sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6=0 net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra=0 2>/dev/null\n    brctl addbr \"$MGMT_BR\"\n    brctl setfd \"$MGMT_BR\" 0 2>/dev/null\n    echo 16384 > \"$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR/bridge/group_fwd_mask\" 2>/dev/null\n    ip link set \"$MGMT_BR\" address \"52:54:01:$node_id:00\"\n    ip link set tap0 mtu \"$_mtu\"\n    ip link set \"$MGMT_BR\" mtu \"$_mtu\"\n    # eth0 joins the bridge only once ether1 is configured (mgmt_attach): until\n    # then nothing the router sends (its boot-time router advertisements, CHR's\n    # DHCP discovers) reaches the management network.\n    brctl addif \"$MGMT_BR\" tap0\n    sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.eth0.disable_ipv6=1 net.ipv6.conf.tap0.disable_ipv6=1 \\\n        \"net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.disable_ipv6=0\" \"net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.accept_ra=0\" \\\n        \"net.ipv6.conf.$MGMT_BR.router_solicitations=0\" 2>/dev/null\nfi\nip link set tap0 up\nip link set \"$MGMT_BR\" up\n# RouterOS's ether1 link-local address, from the MAC this script gives it\nVM_LL=\"fe80::5054:ff:fe${node_id%%:*}:${node_id##*:}00\"\nVM_EP=\"$VM_LL%$MGMT_BR\"\n# The bridge's own link-local address (the startup-config fetch source). Read\n# once qemu runs: until then tap0, the bridge's only port, has no carrier and\n# the address stays tentative.\nLL=\"\"\nbridge_ll() {\n    _w=0\n    while [ -z \"$LL\" ] && [ \"$_w\" -lt 20 ]; do\n        LL=\"$(ip -6 addr show dev \"$MGMT_BR\" 2>/dev/null | grep -v tentative \\\n            | sed -n 's/^ *inet6 \\(fe80::[^/]*\\)\\/64 .*/\\1/p' | head -n1)\"\n        [ -n \"$LL\" ] || { sleep 1; _w=$((_w + 1)); }\n    done\n    [ -n \"$LL\" ] || log \"no IPv6 link-local on $MGMT_BR\"\n}\n\n# NIC order = PCI order = the order of the -device args below. Walk\n# eth1..ethMAX so a gap (links on ether2 and ether5 only) keeps RouterOS\n# numbering aligned: a missing ethN still gets a tap, just no bridge. The count\n# never shrinks across restarts: a `docker restart` recreates the netns and\n# every lab veth of the node is gone, and a NIC absent for one boot loses the\n# config bound to it. The tap keeps ether(N+1) a real interface, its link comes\n# back when containerlab restores the veth or the lab is redeployed.\nmax=0\nfor d in \"$SYSNET\"/eth[1-9]*; do\n    [ -e \"$d\" ] || continue\n    n=\"${d##*/eth}\"\n    [ \"$n\" -gt \"$max\" ] && max=\"$n\"\ndone\nprev=\"$(cat \"$NICS_FILE\" 2>/dev/null)\"\ncase \"$prev\" in *[!0-9]*|\"\") prev=0 ;; esac\n[ \"$prev\" -gt \"$max\" ] && max=\"$prev\"\n# The wait above can end short of CLAB_INTFS on a large lab (links attach after\n# every container started): the NIC set still spans the expected count, and\n# the watcher bridges the late veths.\ncase \"$INTFS\" in *[!0-9]*|\"\") INTFS=0 ;; esac\n[ \"$INTFS\" -gt \"$max\" ] && max=\"$INTFS\"\n[ \"$max\" -gt \"$prev\" ] && { printf '%s\\n' \"$max\" > \"$NICS_FILE\" 2>/dev/null || true; }\n\n# RouterOS v7 memory ≈ 256 + 8·CPUS·(ifaces) MiB (MikroTik CHR system\n# requirements). Scale by the HIGHEST generated NIC, not CLAB_INTFS: a sparse\n# link on ether64 means CLAB_INTFS=1 yet 63 data NICs are created below.\nif [ -z \"${MEM:-}\" ]; then\n    MEM=$((256 + 8 * CPUS * max))\nfi\n\nbridge_eth() { # bridge_eth <i>: container ethI joins brI beside tapI (brI made once)\n    _mtu=\"$(cat \"$SYSNET/eth$1/mtu\" 2>/dev/null || echo 1500)\"\n    if [ ! -e \"$SYSNET/br$1\" ]; then\n        brctl addbr \"br$1\"\n        ip link set \"br$1\" mtu \"$_mtu\"\n        ip link set \"tap$1\" mtu \"$_mtu\"\n        # forward LLDP (01:80:c2:00:00:0e, bit 14); STP/LACP cannot cross a bridge\n        echo 16384 > \"$SYSNET/br$1/bridge/group_fwd_mask\" 2>/dev/null\n        brctl addif \"br$1\" \"tap$1\"\n    fi\n    brctl addif \"br$1\" \"eth$1\"\n    ip link set \"eth$1\" up\n    ip link set \"br$1\" up\n}\n# A veth that lands or returns while qemu runs (containerlab restores a link\n# right after a restart --node, a large lab attaches late, a peer node's\n# redeploy recreates the pair) joins its bridge as it appears, so the RouterOS\n# interface behind tapN gets its link back without a restart here.\nwatch_links() {\n    _warned=\"\"\n    while kill -0 \"$QEMU_PID\" 2>/dev/null; do\n        i=1\n        while [ \"$i\" -le \"$max\" ]; do\n            if [ -e \"$SYSNET/eth$i\" ] && [ ! -e \"$SYSNET/br$i/brif/eth$i\" ]; then\n                bridge_eth \"$i\" && log \"link eth$i attached: bridged to tap$i\"\n            fi\n            i=$((i + 1))\n        done\n        for d in \"$SYSNET\"/eth[1-9]*; do\n            [ -e \"$d\" ] || continue\n            n=\"${d##*/eth}\"\n            [ \"$n\" -gt \"$max\" ] || continue\n            case \" $_warned \" in *\" $n \"*) continue ;; esac\n            _warned=\"$_warned $n\"\n            log \"link eth$n attached after qemu started with $max data NICs: no RouterOS interface for it until the node is restarted\"\n        done\n        sleep 2\n    done\n}\n\ni=1\nwhile [ \"$i\" -le \"$max\" ]; do\n    tap=\"tap$i\"\n    tunctl -t \"$tap\" >/dev/null 2>&1 || ip tuntap add dev \"$tap\" mode tap\n    [ -e \"$SYSNET/eth$i\" ] && bridge_eth \"$i\"\n    ip link set \"$tap\" up\n    mac=\"$(printf '52:54:00:%s:%02x' \"$node_id\" \"$((i & 255))\")\"\n    NET=\"$NET -netdev tap,id=d$i,ifname=$tap,script=no,downscript=no -device virtio-net,netdev=d$i,mac=$mac\"\n    i=$((i + 1))\ndone\n\n# shellcheck disable=SC2086\n$QEMU $ACCEL -display none -monitor none \\\n    -m \"$MEM\" -smp \"cpus=$CPUS\" \\\n    -drive \"file=$IMG,format=raw\" \\\n    -serial telnet:0.0.0.0:5000,server,nowait \\\n    $NET &\nQEMU_PID=$!\ntrap 'kill \"$QEMU_PID\" 2>/dev/null; wait \"$QEMU_PID\" 2>/dev/null; exit 0' TERM INT\nlog \"qemu started (pid $QEMU_PID, mem ${MEM}M, cpus $CPUS, data nics $max)\"\nwatch_links &\n\n# ---- REST helpers ---------------------------------------------------------\njson_str() { printf '%s' \"$1\" | sed 's/\\\\/\\\\\\\\/g; s/\"/\\\\\"/g'; }\nrest() { # rest <user:pass> <path> [json]\n    # Basic auth in a header, never in the URL: a password containing a URI\n    # delimiter (#, ?, /) would change where the authority ends. REST_T is the\n    # read timeout (default 20s).\n    _auth=\"Authorization: Basic $(printf '%s' \"$1\" | base64 | tr -d '\\n')\"\n    if [ $# -ge 3 ]; then\n        wget -q -O- -T \"${REST_T:-20}\" --header \"Content-Type: application/json\" \\\n            --header \"$_auth\" --post-data \"$3\" \"http://[$VM_EP]/rest/$2\" 2>/dev/null\n    else\n        wget -q -O- -T \"${REST_T:-20}\" --header \"$_auth\" \"http://[$VM_EP]/rest/$2\" 2>/dev/null\n    fi\n}\n# busybox wget discards the body of an HTTP error response, and RouterOS puts\n# its diagnosis ONLY there ({\"detail\":\"Script Error: … (line N column M)\"}; its\n# /log stays silent). So the calls whose failure must be readable go over a raw\n# HTTP POST through busybox nc. busybox nc exits the moment stdin hits EOF,\n# reply or not, and RouterOS keeps the connection open despite\n# `Connection: close`, so the request side is held open on a fifo and closed\n# once Content-Length bytes of body have arrived.\nresp_complete() { # resp_complete <file>: headers + Content-Length bytes of body arrived\n    _cl=\"$(grep -i -m1 '^Content-Length:' \"$1\" 2>/dev/null | tr -dc '0-9')\"\n    [ -n \"$_cl\" ] || return 1\n    grep -q -m1 '^\\r*$' \"$1\" 2>/dev/null || return 1\n    [ \"$(sed '1,/^\\r*$/d' \"$1\" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')\" -ge \"$_cl\" ]\n}\nrest_raw() { # rest_raw <user:pass> <path> <json> <timeout-s>  -> \"<status> <body>\"\n    _f=\"/tmp/chr-rest.$$\"; rm -f \"$_f\" \"$_f.out\"; mkfifo \"$_f\" || return 1\n    timeout \"$(( $4 + 5 ))\" nc \"$VM_EP\" 80 <\"$_f\" >\"$_f.out\" 2>/dev/null &\n    _pid=$!\n    exec 7>\"$_f\"\n    printf 'POST /rest/%s HTTP/1.1\\r\\nHost: [%s]\\r\\nAuthorization: Basic %s\\r\\nContent-Type: application/json\\r\\nContent-Length: %s\\r\\nConnection: close\\r\\n\\r\\n%s' \\\n        \"$2\" \"$VM_LL\" \"$(printf '%s' \"$1\" | base64 | tr -d '\\n')\" \\\n        \"$(printf '%s' \"$3\" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')\" \"$3\" >&7\n    _left=$4\n    while kill -0 \"$_pid\" 2>/dev/null && ! resp_complete \"$_f.out\" && [ \"$_left\" -gt 0 ]; do\n        sleep 1; _left=$(( _left - 1 ))\n    done\n    exec 7>&-\n    wait \"$_pid\" 2>/dev/null\n    _st=\"$(head -n1 \"$_f.out\" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\\r' | cut -d' ' -f2)\"\n    _body=\"$(sed '1,/^\\r*$/d' \"$_f.out\" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\\r')\"\n    rm -f \"$_f\" \"$_f.out\"\n    printf '%s %s' \"${_st:-000}\" \"$_body\"\n}\n# RouterOS REST returns the object/array on success and an empty body for a\n# bare `set`: only an explicit error object is a failure here. A silently\n# failed call is caught by the read-back checks that follow each step.\nis_err() { case \"$1\" in *'\"error\"'*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac; }\n\n# ---- wait for RouterOS ----------------------------------------------------\nwaited=0\nAUTH=\"\"\n# A fresh official CHR disk has ONLY the factory `admin` account (blank\n# password): the first boot authenticates as that account whatever --username\n# asks for, and the requested user is created below. On a restart the pair that\n# answers is the requested user.\nwhile [ -z \"$AUTH\" ]; do\n    for _cred in \"admin:\" \"admin:$PASSWORD\" \"$USERNAME:$PASSWORD\"; do\n        rest \"$_cred\" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 && { AUTH=\"$_cred\"; break; }\n    done\n    [ -n \"$AUTH\" ] && break\n    if ! kill -0 \"$QEMU_PID\" 2>/dev/null; then\n        log \"qemu exited during boot\"\n        exit 1\n    fi\n    sleep 2\n    waited=$((waited + 2))\n    if [ \"$waited\" -ge \"$BOOT_WAIT\" ]; then\n        log \"RouterOS did not answer within ${BOOT_WAIT}s: leaving qemu running\"\n        wait \"$QEMU_PID\"\n        exit 1\n    fi\ndone\nlog \"RouterOS answered after ${waited}s\"\n\n# Ready means a user can log in: RouterOS starts its SSH server well after REST\n# answers on a slow boot (about 40 s later under TCG on arm64), so when the\n# configuration keeps SSH enabled, its port must send the banner first.\n# A config that disables SSH is not waited for; a banner that never comes is\n# logged and the node is still declared ready (REST works).\nssh_banner() { (sleep 3) | nc \"$VM_EP\" 22 2>/dev/null | head -c 7; }\nready() {\n    case \"$(rest \"$AUTH\" \"ip/service?name=ssh\")\" in\n        *'\"disabled\":\"false\"'*)\n            _t0=$(date +%s)\n            until [ \"$(ssh_banner)\" = \"SSH-2.0\" ]; do\n                if [ $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 )) -ge \"$BOOT_WAIT\" ]; then\n                    log \"SSH did not answer within $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 ))s (REST works)\"\n                    break\n                fi\n                sleep 2\n            done\n            ;;\n    esac\n    touch \"$READY_FILE\" 2>/dev/null || true\n    log \"RouterOS ready\"\n}\n\n# A failed step WITHHOLDS the ready marker (qemu keeps running, so the node can\n# still be inspected over the serial console, port 5000 in the container).\nbootstrap_fail() {\n    log \"credential bootstrap FAILED: $1\"\n    wait \"$QEMU_PID\"\n    exit 0\n}\n\n# ---- management: ether1 in its own VRF -------------------------------------\n# The VRF owns its routing table and connected routes. Services must bind to\n# it explicitly; source-policy rules are unnecessary. The link-local REST\n# channel survives the handoff once www and ether1 belong to the same VRF.\nmgmt_fail() {\n    log \"management setup FAILED: $1 (redeploy the node: containerlab deploy --reconfigure)\"\n    wait \"$QEMU_PID\"\n    exit 0\n}\nrest_has() { # rest_has <path?query>: the GET answered a non-empty JSON array\n    case \"$(rest \"$AUTH\" \"$1\")\" in '['*'{'*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac\n}\nrest_add() { # rest_add <what> <path> <json>: a 2xx with no error object, else mgmt_fail with the router's detail\n    _r=\"$(rest_raw \"$AUTH\" \"$2\" \"$3\" 20)\"\n    case \"$_r\" in\n        2??\\ *) is_err \"$_r\" && mgmt_fail \"$1: ${_r#* }\" ;;\n        *) mgmt_fail \"$1: ${_r:-no response}\" ;;\n    esac\n}\nrest_count() { # rest_count <path?query>: number of objects the GET answered\n    rest \"$AUTH\" \"$1\" | tr '{' '\\n' | grep -c '\"\\.id\"'\n}\nrest_clear() { # rest_clear <menu>: remove its clab-mgmt objects\n    _ids=\"$(rest \"$AUTH\" \"$1?comment=$MGMT_COMMENT\" | tr '{' '\\n' \\\n        | sed -n 's/.*\"\\.id\":\"\\([^\"]*\\)\".*/\\1/p' | paste -sd, -)\"\n    [ -z \"$_ids\" ] || rest_add \"remove old $1\" \"$1/remove\" \"{\\\".id\\\":\\\"$_ids\\\"}\"\n}\n# A native VRF creates its routing table asynchronously. 441: # ---- management: ether1 addressing and its own routing table ----------------
442: # ether1 gets the container's management addresses, and their return path lives
443: # in a `mgmt` routing table selected by a rule on those source addresses: a
444: # default route the lab adds to `main` (a static 0.0.0.0/0, a PPPoE client's
445: # default route, a dual-WAN pair) would otherwise take SSH/REST replies away
446: # from the management network while the data plane works. CHR's default ether1
447: # DHCP client is disabled: the address is static. Everything is tagged
448: # clab-mgmt and re-applied on every boot from the container's CURRENT addressing
449: # (a restart can bring a new IP), while the bootstrap channel itself
450: # (link-local) never depends on it.

452:     log "management setup FAILED: $1 (redeploy the node: containerlab deploy --reconfigure)"

549: }
550: # Join the management network, then have the router reach its gateway from the
551: # management address: proves the return path both ways, and the ARP/ND request
552: # refreshes the gateway's neighbor entry when the IP was used by another MAC
553: # before (a redeployed lab hands out the same addresses).
554: mgmt_attach() {
555:     [ -e "$SYSNET/$MGMT_BR/brif/eth0" ] || brctl addif "$MGMT_BR" eth0
556:     ip link set eth0 up
557:     for _pair in "$G4 ${M4%/*}" "$G6 ${M6%/*}"; do
558:         # shellcheck disable=SC2086  # split "gateway source"; an empty half skips the pair
559:         set -- $_pair
560:         [ $# -eq 2 ] || continue
561:         _t0=$(date +%s)
562:         until case "$(rest "$AUTH" ping "{\"address\":\"$1\",\"src-address\":\"$2\",\"count\":\"2\"}")" in
563:                 *'"received":"'[1-9]*) true ;; *) false ;; esac; do
564:             if [ $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 )) -ge 30 ]; then
565:                 log "gateway $1 does not answer from $2 after $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 ))s (continuing)"
566:                 break
567:             fi
568:             sleep 1
569:         done
570:     done
571: }
572: 
573: # Bootstrap + startup-config import happen ONCE per container lifetime. On a
574: # restart the CHR disk keeps its config and the marker (in the container rw
575: # layer) survives, so the bootstrap (which could wait forever if the config
576: # disabled `www` or changed the account, or reject duplicate `add` lines) is
577: # skipped. A fresh deploy recreates the container and the disk, so the marker
578: # and the config are both gone and the bootstrap runs.
579: if [ -f "$DONE_MARKER" ]; then
580:     log "already bootstrapped (restart): skipping config"
581:     mgmt_setup
582:     mgmt_attach
583:     ready
584:     wait "$QEMU_PID"
585:     exit 0
586: fi
587: 
588: # ---- credentials + identity -----------------------------------------------
589: # Every credential-establishing call is CHECKED: the ready marker never
590: # advertises credentials that do not work.
591: FACTORY="admin:"
592: rest "$FACTORY" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 || FACTORY="admin:$PASSWORD"
593: if [ "$USERNAME" = "admin" ]; then
594:     if [ -n "$PASSWORD" ]; then
595:         out="$(rest "$FACTORY" user/set \
596:             "{\"numbers\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"$(json_str "$PASSWORD")\"}")"
597:         is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "set admin password: ${out:-no response}"
598:     fi
599:     AUTH="admin:$PASSWORD"
600: else
601:     out="$(rest "$FACTORY" user/add \
602:         "{\"name\":\"$(json_str "$USERNAME")\",\"password\":\"$(json_str "$PASSWORD")\",\"group\":\"full\"}")"
603:     is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "create user $USERNAME: ${out:-no response}"
604:     AUTH="$USERNAME:$PASSWORD"
605:     # The factory `admin` still has a BLANK password and is reachable over the
606:     # forwarded services: disable it so the node keeps no unauthenticated
607:     # full-access account.
608:     out="$(rest "$AUTH" user/set "{\"numbers\":\"admin\",\"disabled\":\"yes\"}")"
609:     is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "disable factory admin: ${out:-no response}"
610:     if rest "admin:" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1; then
611:         bootstrap_fail "factory admin still authenticates after disable"
612:     fi
613: fi
614: rest "$AUTH" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 \
615:     || bootstrap_fail "the requested credentials do not authenticate"
616: out="$(rest "$AUTH" system/identity/set "{\"name\":\"$(json_str "$HOSTNAME_ARG")\"}")"
617: is_err "$out" && bootstrap_fail "set identity: ${out:-no response}"
618: got="$(rest "$AUTH" system/identity)"
619: case "$got" in
620:     *"\"name\":\"$HOSTNAME_ARG\""*) : ;;
621:     *) bootstrap_fail "identity not applied: ${got:-no response}" ;;
622: esac
623: 
624: mgmt_setup
625: mgmt_attach
626: 
627: # ---- startup config -------------------------------------------------------
628: if [ -s "$STARTUP_CFG" ]; then
629:     bridge_ll
630:     # one-shot HTTP server on the bridge's link-local address; the router
631:     # fetches from it through ether1 (fetch takes a zoned link-local address
632:     # only as `address=`, not inside a URL)
633:     {
634:         printf 'HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\nContent-Length: %s\r\n\r\n' \
635:             "$(wc -c < "$STARTUP_CFG")"
636:         cat "$STARTUP_CFG"
637:     } | timeout 90 nc -l -s "$LL%$MGMT_BR" -p "$FETCH_PORT" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
638:     sleep 1
639:     fetch="$(rest "$AUTH" tool/fetch \
640:         "{\"address\":\"$LL%ether1\",\"port\":\"$FETCH_PORT\",\"src-path\":\"/config.auto.rsc\",\"mode\":\"http\",\"dst-path\":\"config.auto.rsc\"}")"
641:     case "$fetch" in
642:         *'"status":"finished"'*)
643:             # /import answers only when it finishes: a large config gets
644:             # CHR_BOOT_WAIT seconds.
645:             result="$(rest_raw "$AUTH" import '{"file-name":"config.auto.rsc"}' "$BOOT_WAIT")"
646:             case "$result" in
647:                 *'"ret":"true"'*)
648:                     log "startup config imported"
649:                     ;;
650:                 *)
651:                     # RouterOS imports line by line and stops at the first
652:                     # error: the lines before it ARE applied.
653:                     detail="$(printf '%s' "$result" | sed -n 's/.*"detail":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')"
654:                     log "startup config import FAILED: ${detail:-${result:-no response}}; lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not"
655:                     wait "$QEMU_PID"
656:                     exit 0
657:                     ;;
658:             esac
659:             ;;

*) return 1 ;; esac\n}\nrest_add() { # rest_add <what> <path> <json>: a 2xx with no error object, else mgmt_fail with the router's detail\n    _r=\"$(rest_raw \"$AUTH\" \"$2\" \"$3\" 20)\"\n    case \"$_r\" in\n        2??\\ *) is_err \"$_r\" && mgmt_fail \"$1: ${_r#* }\" ;;\n        *) mgmt_fail \"$1: ${_r:-no response}\" ;;\n    esac\n}\nrest_count() { # rest_count <path?query>: number of objects the GET answered\n    rest \"$AUTH\" \"$1\" | tr '{' '\\n' | grep -c '\"\\.id\"'\n}\nrest_clear() { # rest_clear <menu>: remove its clab-mgmt objects\n    _ids=\"$(rest \"$AUTH\" \"$1?comment=$MGMT_COMMENT\" | tr '{' '\\n' \\\n        | sed -n 's/.*\"\\.id\":\"\\([^\"]*\\)\".*/\\1/p' | paste -sd, -)\"\n    [ -z \"$_ids\" ] || rest_add \"remove old $1\" \"$1/remove\" \"{\\\".id\\\":\\\"$_ids\\\"}\"\n}\n# The tagged objects already match the container's addressing (a restart with\n# the same IP): leave them alone, re-applying would only drop live sessions.\nmgmt_in_place() {\n    _want=0\n    if [ -n \"$M4\" ]; *) false ;; esac; do\n            if [ $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 )) -ge 30 ]; then\n                log \"gateway $1 does not answer from $2 after $(( $(date +%s) - _t0 ))s (continuing)\"\n                break\n            fi\n            sleep 1\n        done\n    done\n}\n\n# Bootstrap + startup-config import happen ONCE per container lifetime. On a\n# restart the CHR disk keeps its config and the marker (in the container rw\n# layer) survives, so the bootstrap (which could wait forever if the config\n# disabled `www` or changed the account, or reject duplicate `add` lines) is\n# skipped. A fresh deploy recreates the container and the disk, so the marker\n# and the config are both gone and the bootstrap runs.\nif [ -f \"$DONE_MARKER\" ]; then\n    log \"already bootstrapped (restart): skipping config\"\n    mgmt_setup\n    mgmt_attach\n    ready\n    wait \"$QEMU_PID\"\n    exit 0\nfi\n\n# ---- credentials + identity -----------------------------------------------\n# Every credential-establishing call is CHECKED: the ready marker never\n# advertises credentials that do not work.\nFACTORY=\"admin:\"\nrest \"$FACTORY\" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1 || FACTORY=\"admin:$PASSWORD\"\nif [ \"$USERNAME\" = \"admin\" ]; then\n    if [ -n \"$PASSWORD\" ]; then\n        out=\"$(rest \"$FACTORY\" user/set \\\n            \"{\\\"numbers\\\":\\\"admin\\\",\\\"password\\\":\\\"$(json_str \"$PASSWORD\")\\\"}\")\"\n        is_err \"$out\" && bootstrap_fail \"set admin password: ${out:-no response}\"\n    fi\n    AUTH=\"admin:$PASSWORD\"\nelse\n    out=\"$(rest \"$FACTORY\" user/add \\\n        \"{\\\"name\\\":\\\"$(json_str \"$USERNAME\")\\\",\\\"password\\\":\\\"$(json_str \"$PASSWORD\")\\\",\\\"group\\\":\\\"full\\\"}\")\"\n    is_err \"$out\" && bootstrap_fail \"create user $USERNAME: ${out:-no response}\"\n    AUTH=\"$USERNAME:$PASSWORD\"\n    # The factory `admin` still has a BLANK password and is reachable over the\n    # forwarded services: disable it so the node keeps no unauthenticated\n    # full-access account.\n    out=\"$(rest \"$AUTH\" user/set \"{\\\"numbers\\\":\\\"admin\\\",\\\"disabled\\\":\\\"yes\\\"}\")\"\n    is_err \"$out\" && bootstrap_fail \"disable factory admin: ${out:-no response}\"\n    if rest \"admin:\" system/resource >/dev/null 2>&1; 5: // Package mikrotik_chr runs MikroTik RouterOS CHR from the official mikrotik/chr image.
6: //
7: // The image is MikroTik's own distribution (Alpine + qemu + the CHR disk) and is used
8: // unmodified: the kind writes chr-launch.sh into the node's lab directory, bind-mounts it
9: // read-only and sets it as the entrypoint in place of the image's /start.sh, which is not
10: // orchestration-ready (containerlab#3116, #3464).
11: package mikrotik_chr
12: 
13: import (
14: 	"context"
15: 	_ "embed"
16: 	"fmt"
17: 	"net"
18: 	"os"
19: 	"path"
20: 	"path/filepath"
21: 	"regexp"

33: 	kindNames          = []string{"mikrotik_chr"}
34: 	defaultCredentials = clabnodes.NewCredentials("admin", "admin")
35: 
36: 	InterfaceRegexp = regexp.MustCompile(`ether(?P<port>\d+)`)
37: 	InterfaceOffset = 2
38: 	InterfaceHelp   = "etherX (where X >= 2) or ethX (where X >= 1)"
39: 
40: 	//go:embed chr-launch.sh
41: 	launcherScript []byte
42: )

44: const (
45: 	configDirName   = "ftpboot"
46: 	startupCfgFName = "config.auto.rsc"
47: 
48: 	launcherFName = "chr-launch.sh"
49: 	launcherPath  = "/chr-launch.sh"
50: 	// readyFile is written by the launcher once RouterOS accepted the credentials and the
51: 	// startup config, and removed at every container start.
52: 	readyFile = "/.chr-launch-ready"
53: 
54: 	// mgmtComment tags every management object the launcher creates in RouterOS.
55: 	mgmtComment = "clab-mgmt"
56: 
57: 	// the launcher's CHR_INTF_WAIT and CHR_BOOT_WAIT defaults, and the time its config
58: 	// fetch and gateway check add, in seconds.
59: 	defaultIntfWait  = 60
60: 	defaultBootWait  = 300

66: // Register registers the node in the NodeRegistry.
67: func Register(r *clabnodes.NodeRegistry) {
68: 	platformAttrs := &clabnodes.PlatformAttrs{
69: 		ScrapliPlatformName: scrapliPlatformName,
70: 	}
71: 
72: 	nrea := clabnodes.NewNodeRegistryEntryAttributes(defaultCredentials, nil, platformAttrs)
73: 
74: 	r.Register(kindNames, func() clabnodes.Node {
75: 		return new(mikrotikCHR)
76: 	}, nrea)
77: }

79: type mikrotikCHR struct {
80: 	clabnodes.VRNode
81: }
82: 
83: func (n *mikrotikCHR) Init(cfg *clabtypes.NodeConfig, opts ...clabnodes.NodeOption) error {
84: 	n.VRNode = *clabnodes.NewVRNode(n, defaultCredentials, scrapliPlatformName)
85: 	n.ConfigDirName = configDirName
86: 	n.StartupCfgFName = startupCfgFName
87: 	// The image's qemu falls back to TCG emulation without /dev/kvm: KVM makes the boot
88: 	// fast but is not required.
89: 	n.HostRequirements.VirtRequired = false
90: 
91: 	n.Cfg = cfg
92: 	for _, o := range opts {
93: 		o(n)
94: 	}
95: 
96: 	// Credentials travel as env, not on the command line, so a password needs no quoting.
97: 	defEnv := map[string]string{
98: 		"USERNAME": n.Cfg.Credentials.Username,
99: 		"PASSWORD": n.Cfg.Credentials.Password,
100: 	}
101: 	n.Cfg.Env = clabutils.MergeStringMaps(defEnv, n.Cfg.Env)
102: 
103: 	n.Cfg.Binds = append(n.Cfg.Binds,
104: 		fmt.Sprint(path.Join(n.Cfg.LabDir, configDirName), ":/ftpboot"),
105: 		fmt.Sprint(path.Join(n.Cfg.LabDir, launcherFName), ":", launcherPath, ":ro"),
106: 	)
107: 
108: 	if n.Cfg.Entrypoint == "" {
109: 		n.Cfg.Entrypoint = "/bin/sh " + launcherPath
110: 	}
111: 	n.Cfg.Cmd = fmt.Sprintf("--hostname %s", n.Cfg.ShortName)
112: 
113: 	if n.Cfg.Healthcheck == nil {
114: 		n.Cfg.Healthcheck = &clabtypes.HealthcheckConfig{
115: 			Test:        []string{"CMD-SHELL", "test -f " + readyFile},
116: 			Interval:    5,
117: 			Timeout:     3,
118: 			Retries:     3,
119: 			StartPeriod: startPeriod(n.Cfg.Env),
120: 		}
121: 	}
122: 
123: 	n.InterfaceRegexp = InterfaceRegexp
124: 	n.InterfaceOffset = InterfaceOffset
125: 	n.InterfaceHelp = InterfaceHelp
126: 
127: 	return nil
128: }
129: 
130: // startPeriod is the healthcheck start period in seconds: the launcher's own worst case
131: // before the ready file, so a slow boot (TCG) never reports unhealthy. It waits up to
132: // CHR_INTF_WAIT for the links, then up to CHR_BOOT_WAIT each for REST, the VRF
133: // handoff, the startup-config import and the SSH banner, plus fetch and gateway checks.
134: func startPeriod(env map[string]string) int {
135: 	return envSeconds(env, "CHR_INTF_WAIT", defaultIntfWait) +
136: 		4*envSeconds(env, "CHR_BOOT_WAIT", defaultBootWait) + startPeriodSlack
137: }
138: 
139: // envSeconds reads a positive number of seconds from env, else returns def (the launcher
140: // falls back to its default the same way).
141: func envSeconds(env map[string]string, key string, def int) int {
142: 	if v, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(env[key])); err == nil && v > 0 {
143: 		return v
144: 	}
145: 
146: 	return def
147: }
148: 
149: // PreDeploy writes the launcher next to the startup config on every deploy, so a
150: // containerlab upgrade ships its launcher to existing labs.
151: func (n *mikrotikCHR) PreDeploy(ctx context.Context, params *clabnodes.PreDeployParams) error {
152: 	if err := n.VRNode.PreDeploy(ctx, params); err != nil {
153: 		return err
154: 	}
155: 
156: 	dst := filepath.Join(n.Cfg.LabDir, launcherFName)
157: 	if err := os.WriteFile(dst, launcherScript, clabconstants.PermissionsFileDefault); err != nil {
158: 		return fmt.Errorf("node %q: failed to write %s: %w", n.Cfg.ShortName, dst, err)
159: 	}
160: 
161: 	return nil
162: }
163: 
164: // PreStop skips VRNode's vrnetlab qcow2 alias step, which does not apply to this image.
165: func (*mikrotikCHR) PreStop(_ context.Context) error {
166: 	return nil
167: }

169: // SaveConfig exports the RouterOS configuration over SSH (scrapligo has no RouterOS
170: // platform, see clabnodes.ExportConfigOverSSH) and writes it as the node's startup config,
171: // without the objects the launcher creates at every boot. Verbose service settings
172: // retain a user override back to main, which compact export omits as a RouterOS default.
173: func (n *mikrotikCHR) SaveConfig(_ context.Context) (*clabnodes.SaveConfigResult, error) {
174: 	exported, err := clabnodes.ExportConfigOverSSH(
175: 		net.JoinHostPort(n.Cfg.LongName, "22"),
176: 		n.Cfg.Credentials.Username,
177: 		n.Cfg.Credentials.Password,
178: 		`/export; :put "# clab-service-defaults"; /ip service export verbose; /snmp export verbose`,
179: 	)
180: 	if err != nil {
181: 		return nil, err
182: 	}
183: 
184: 	return clabnodes.WriteSavedConfig(n.Cfg, n.ConfigDirName, n.StartupCfgFName,
185: 		[]byte(filterLauncherConfig(exported)+"\n"))
186: }
187: 
188: // filterLauncherConfig drops what the launcher configures at every boot from an /export:
189: // every object tagged clab-mgmt (the ether1 management addresses, the mgmt VRF
190: // and its default routes), the ether1 ND entry and CHR's ether1 DHCP client. Imported again
191: // as a startup config, these lines duplicate objects the launcher already created and
192: // RouterOS stops the import at the first one; the management addressing also belongs to
193: // the deployment, not the lab. Continuation lines (an unescaped trailing backslash) are joined
194: // before
195: // matching.
196: func filterLauncherConfig(config string) string {
197: 	var out []string
198: 
199: 	section := ""
200: 	pending := ""
201: 	serviceDefaults := false
202: 	for line := range strings.SplitSeq(strings.ReplaceAll(config, "\r\n", "\n"), "\n") {
203: 		if pending != "" {
204: 			line = pending + "\n" + line
205: 			pending = ""
206: 		}
207: 		if continues(line) {
208: 			pending = line
209: 			continue
210: 		}
211: 
212: 		trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(line)
213: 		if trimmed == "# clab-service-defaults" {
214: 			serviceDefaults = true
215: 			continue
216: 		}
217: 		if strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "/") {
218: 			section = trimmed
219: 		}
220: 		// The verbose tail supplies service defaults only. In particular, SNMP
221: 		// communities were already exported: adding them twice would fail import.
222: 		if serviceDefaults && section != "/ip service" && section != "/snmp" {
223: 			continue
224: 		}
225: 		if launcherOwned(section, trimmed) {
226: 			continue
227: 		}
228: 		out = append(out, line)
229: 	}
230: 	if pending != "" {
231: 		out = append(out, pending)
232: 	}
233: 
234: 	return strings.Join(out, "\n")
235: }
236: 
237: // continues reports whether an /export line continues on the next one: it ends in an
238: // unescaped backslash. RouterOS writes a literal backslash in a value as `\\`, so an even
239: // run of trailing backslashes ends the line.
240: func continues(line string) bool {
241: 	trailing := len(line) - len(strings.TrimRight(line, `\`))
242: 
243: 	return trailing%2 == 1
244: }
245: 
246: func launcherOwned(section, line string) bool {
247: 	if !strings.HasPrefix(line, "add ") {
248: 		return false
249: 	}
250: 
251: 	fields := strings.Fields(strings.ReplaceAll(line, `\`, " "))
252: 	has := func(kv string) bool { return slices.Contains(fields, kv) }
253: 
254: 	if has("comment=" + mgmtComment) {
255: 		return true
256: 	}
257: 
258: 	// /ipv6 nd keeps no comment: the launcher's ether1 entry is matched by interface.
259: 	switch section {

147: func TestInterfaceParsing(t *testing.T) {
148: 	tests := map[string]struct {
149: 		ifaces  []string
150: 		want    []string
151: 		wantErr bool
152: 	}{
153: 		"routeros-names": {
154: 			ifaces: []string{"ether2", "ether5", "ether13"},
155: 			want:   []string{"eth1", "eth4", "eth12"},
156: 		},
157: 		"eth-names":   {ifaces: []string{"eth1", "eth3"}, want: []string{"eth1", "eth3"}},
158: 		"mgmt-ether1": {ifaces: []string{"ether1"}, wantErr: true},
159: 	}
160: 
161: 	for name, tc := range tests {
162: 		t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T) {
163: 			n := newInitialized(t, &clabtypes.NodeConfig{ShortName: "r1", LabDir: t.TempDir()})
164: 
165: 			var err error
166: 			for _, ifName := range tc.ifaces {
167: 				ep := &clablinks.EndpointVeth{
168: 					EndpointGeneric: clablinks.EndpointGeneric{IfaceName: ifName},
169: 				}
170: 				if err = n.AddEndpoint(ep); err != nil {
171: 					break
172: 				}
173: 			}
174: 			if err == nil {
175: 				err = n.CheckInterfaceName()
176: 			}
177: 
178: 			if tc.wantErr {
179: 				if err == nil {
180: 					t.Fatalf("interfaces %v: want an error, got none", tc.ifaces)
181: 				}
182: 				return
183: 			}
184: 			if err != nil {
185: 				t.Fatalf("interfaces %v: %v", tc.ifaces, err)
186: 			}
187: 			for i, ep := range n.Endpoints {
188: 				if ep.GetIfaceName() != tc.want[i] {
189: 					t.Errorf(
190: 						"%q mapped to %q, want %q",
191: 						tc.ifaces[i],
192: 						ep.GetIfaceName(),
193: 						tc.want[i],
194: 					)
195: 				}
196: 			}
197: 		})
198: 	}
199: }

243: func TestFilterLauncherConfig(t *testing.T) {
244: 	got := filterLauncherConfig(exportedConfig)
245: 
246: 	if strings.Contains(got, "clab-mgmt") {
247: 		t.Errorf("filtered config still contains a clab-mgmt object:\n%s", got)
248: 	}
249: 	for _, gone := range []string{
250: 		"add disabled=yes interface=ether1 name=client1",
251: 		"add interface=ether1 ra-lifetime=none",
252: 		"172.20.20.4",
253: 		"3fff:172:20:20::4",
254: 	} {
255: 		if strings.Contains(got, gone) {
256: 			t.Errorf("filtered config still contains launcher line %q:\n%s", gone, got)
257: 		}
258: 	}
259: 
260: 	for _, kept := range []string{
261: 		"add address=10.0.0.2/30 interface=ether2 network=10.0.0.0",
262: 		"add address=2.2.2.2 interface=lo0 network=2.2.2.2",
263: 		"add dst-address=0.0.0.0/0 gateway=10.0.0.1",
264: 		"add name=lo0",
265: 		"set name=r2",
266: 		"/routing table",

294: func TestFilterLauncherConfigEscapedBackslash(t *testing.T) {
295: 	// A value ending in a literal backslash is exported as `\\`: that line is complete and
296: 	// must not swallow the launcher line after it.
297: 	in := "/ip address\n" +
298: 		"add address=10.9.9.1/24 interface=ether2 network=10.9.9.0 comment=path\\\\\n" +
299: 		"add address=172.20.20.3/24 comment=clab-mgmt interface=ether1 network=\\\n" +
300: 		"    172.20.20.0\n"
301: 
302: 	got := filterLauncherConfig(in)
303: 
304: 	if !strings.Contains(
305: 		got,
306: 		"add address=10.9.9.1/24 interface=ether2 network=10.9.9.0 comment=path",
307: 	) {
308: 		t.Errorf("user address ending in an escaped backslash was dropped:\n%s", got)
309: 	}
310: 	if strings.Contains(got, "clab-mgmt") {
311: 		t.Errorf("launcher address kept:\n%s", got)
312: 	}
313: }

315: func TestContinues(t *testing.T) {
316: 	for line, want := range map[string]bool{
317: 		`add a=b`:     false,
318: 		`add a=b \`:   true,
319: 		`add a=b\\`:   false,
320: 		`add a=b\\ \`: true,
321: 		`add a=b\\\`:  true,
322: 		`add a=b\\\\`: false,
323: 	} {
324: 		if got := continues(line); got != want {
325: 			t.Errorf("continues(%q) = %v, want %v", line, got, want)
326: 		}

1: ---
2: search:
3:   boost: 4
4: kind_code_name: mikrotik_chr
5: kind_display_name: MikroTik RouterOS CHR
6: ---
7: # -{{ kind_display_name }}-
8: 
9: [MikroTik RouterOS](https://mikrotik.com/software) Cloud Hosted Router (CHR) from the **official [`mikrotik/chr`](https://hub.docker.com/r/mikrotik/chr) image** is identified with the `-{{ kind_code_name }}-` kind in the [topology file](../topo-def-file.md). The image is published by MikroTik for `amd64` and `arm64` and is used as is: no [vrnetlab](../vrnetlab.md) build is needed.
10: 
11: The image is a QEMU VM (Alpine, qemu and the CHR disk) in a container. Its own `/start.sh` is not made for orchestrated links ([#3116](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/issues/3116)), so the kind writes a launcher script into the node's lab directory, mounts it read-only and runs it as the entrypoint instead. The launcher uses only the tools that ship in the image.
12: 
13: /// note
14: The [`mikrotik_ros`](vr-ros.md) kind runs CHR from an image you build with vrnetlab. Both kinds use the same interface naming and startup config format, so a lab moves from one to the other by changing `kind` and `image`.
15: ///
16: 
17: ## Getting -{{ kind_display_name }}- image
18: 
19: ```bash
20: docker pull mikrotik/chr:7.24.5
21: ```
22: 
23: Tags follow RouterOS versions, plus `stable`, `long-term`, `testing` and `development`. This kind has been tested with 7.24.5 (stable), 7.23.8 (long-term) and 7.25rc2 (testing).
24: 
25: ## Managing -{{ kind_display_name }}- nodes
26: 
27: /// tab | CLI
28: ```bash
29: ssh admin@<node-name>
30: ```
31: ///
32: /// tab | REST API
33: ```bash
34: curl -u admin:admin http://<node-name>/rest/system/resource
35: ```
36: ///
37: /// tab | Winbox / API
38: Winbox (TCP 8291) and the RouterOS API (TCP 8728, 8729 for TLS) are reachable on the node's management address.
39: ///
40: /// tab | Console
41: The serial console is on port 5000 inside the container:
42: ```bash
43: docker exec -it <node-name> nc 127.0.0.1 5000
44: ```
45: ///
46: /// tab | bash
47: ```bash
48: docker exec -it <node-name> sh
49: ```
50: ///
51: 
52: The node's management address is RouterOS's own `ether1` address in the `mgmt` VRF ([transparent management](#management-connectivity)). Services bound to this VRF answer directly, with nothing forwarded.
53: 
54: /// note
55: Default credentials are `admin:admin`. With custom [`credentials`](../nodes.md#credentials) the kind creates that user in the `full` group and disables the factory `admin` account, which has a blank password on a fresh CHR disk.
56: ///
57: 
58: ## Interface naming
59: 
60: You can use [interface names](../topo-def-file.md#interface-naming) in the topology file like they appear in RouterOS: `etherX`, where `X` is the port number.
61: 
62: * `ether2` - first data port
63: * `ether3` - second data port, and so on
64: 
65: /// admonition
66:     type: warning
67: Data ports start at `ether2`: `ether1` is the management interface. Using `ether1` in a topology results in an error.
68: ///
69: 
70: The container interface `ethN` is RouterOS `ether(N+1)`, also when links leave gaps: a link on `eth12` alone still lands on `ether13`, with `ether2` to `ether12` present and unlinked. Interface MTU follows the link MTU, and LLDP frames are forwarded, so `/ip neighbor` shows the peers.
71: 
72: ## Node configuration
73: 
74: -{{ kind_display_name }}- nodes boot with the default CHR configuration plus the credentials, the identity (set to the node name) and the management setup described below.
75: 
76: ### Startup configuration
77: 
78: A RouterOS script (`.rsc`) set with [`startup-config`](../nodes.md#startup-config) is imported once the router is up:
79: 
80: ```yaml
81: name: chr_lab
82: topology:
83:   nodes:
84:     r1:
85:       kind: mikrotik_chr
86:       image: mikrotik/chr:7.24.5
87:       startup-config: r1.rsc
88: ```
89: 
90: The file is copied to the node's lab directory as `ftpboot/config.auto.rsc` and imported over the REST API. RouterOS imports line by line and stops at the first error: in that case the container log carries RouterOS's own reason with the line number, for example
91: 
92: ```
93: chr-launch: startup config import FAILED: Script Error: bad parameter network-type (line 3 column 59); lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not
94: ```
95: 
96: and the node does not become ready.
97: 
98: ### Saving configuration
99: 
100: [`containerlab save`](../../cmd/save.md) writes each node's `/export` to `ftpboot/config.auto.rsc` in its lab directory. The management objects the launcher creates at every boot (everything tagged `clab-mgmt`, and the `ether1` DHCP client) are left out, so the saved file can be used as the startup config of the next deployment, also one with different management addresses. Service settings include their defaults so an explicit VRF override back to `main` survives the next deployment.
101: 
102: ### Node readiness
103: 
104: The node is ready once RouterOS accepted the credentials and the startup config, reaches its gateway from the management address and, unless the configuration disables SSH, its SSH server answers. An SSH server that does not answer within `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` is logged, and the node is still declared ready, since REST and the console work. The container log then shows
105: 
106: ```
107: chr-launch: RouterOS ready
108: ```
109: 
110: and the kind's default [healthcheck](../nodes.md#healthcheck) reports the container `healthy`, so [`stages`](../nodes.md#stages) with `wait-for` can depend on it. A node whose startup config was rejected never becomes healthy. The default healthcheck's start period follows the launcher's own deadlines (`CHR_INTF_WAIT` + 4 × `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` + 90 s, 1350 s with the defaults), so a slow boot never reports `unhealthy`. A `healthcheck` set in the topology replaces the default one.
111: 
112: ### Resources
113: 
114: The kind reads the official image's own environment variables:
115: 
116: | Variable | Default | Purpose |
117: |----------|---------|---------|
118: | `MEM` | 256 MiB + 8 MiB per data interface and vCPU | VM memory (a QEMU `-m` value, e.g. `1024` or `1G`) |
119: | `CPUS` | `1` | VM vCPUs |
120: | `DISK` | `128M` | minimum disk size (the disk only grows) |
121: | `CHR_INTF_WAIT` | `60` | seconds to wait for the data interfaces containerlab attaches before the VM starts |
122: | `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` | `300` | seconds to wait for RouterOS to answer, for the VRF handoff, for the startup config import, and for SSH before the node is declared ready |
123: 
124: ```yaml
125: r1:
126:   kind: mikrotik_chr
127:   image: mikrotik/chr:7.24.5
128:   env:
129:     MEM: 1024
130:     CPUS: 2
131: ```
132: 
133: KVM is used when `/dev/kvm` is available. Without it the image's QEMU runs under TCG emulation: the node works, but boots several times slower.
134: 
135: ## Management connectivity
136: 
137: Management is transparent: the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and gateways containerlab gives the node's `eth0` are configured on RouterOS `ether1`, and the container's `eth0` is bridged to the VM's `ether1`. The address in the topology table is the one in the RouterOS configuration.
138: 
139: The image ships busybox only (no `tc`), so where vrnetlab's [transparent management](../vrnetlab.md#management-interface) redirects with tc-mirred, this kind uses a Linux bridge. The container itself has no address on the management network; it reaches RouterOS for bootstrap over IPv6 link-local on that bridge.
140: 
141: The launcher places `ether1` in a native `mgmt` VRF before `main`. RouterOS creates its routing table and connected routes; the launcher adds IPv4 and IPv6 defaults that resolve their gateways in `mgmt`. No source-policy rules or route leaks are added. Data interfaces remain in `main`, so a lab default route does not take management replies away from `ether1`. CHR's `ether1` DHCP client is disabled.
142: 
143: On first boot, one RouterOS background job creates the VRF and binds SSH, HTTP/HTTPS (including REST), API/API-SSL, Winbox, Telnet and SNMP to it. Their enabled/disabled state is preserved. The launcher waits for the native routing table and service bindings before configuring management addressing, joining the external management bridge and fetching the startup config through `mgmt`. On restart, startup-config service overrides are preserved. The launcher uses HTTP/REST with the topology credentials during container startup. SSH in `mgmt` provides user login access and is also used by `containerlab save`. Credential setup, service ports and access controls are unchanged.
144: 
145: A service's VRF binding also changes where it can be reached: these services no longer listen through data interfaces in `main` unless the startup config changes their binding. RouterOS FTP does not support VRF binding and is unavailable through the management VRF. Other router-originated services, such as DNS, NTP and logging, need their own VRF-aware configuration to use management egress. RouterOS applies its VRF interface matching to firewall rules; see the [RouterOS VRF documentation](https://manual.mikrotik.com/docs/user-guides/routing-and-networking-protocols/vrf/).
146: 
147: VRF membership does not disable Layer 2 neighbor discovery. LLDP, CDP and MNDP follow `/ip neighbor discovery-settings`; use an explicit interface list excluding `ether1` when management discovery is unwanted.
148: 
149: RouterOS's router advertisements on `ether1` carry a zero router lifetime, so no host on the management network takes the router as its IPv6 default gateway. The container joins the management network only once this is in place. Management objects carry the comment `clab-mgmt` and are re-applied at boot when the container's addressing changed.
150: 
151: /// warning
152: Do not remove or change the `clab-mgmt` objects or the `mgmt` VRF: management of the node depends on them. This setup requires a fresh node container; it does not migrate a running node that uses the previous policy-only `mgmt` table. Export the user configuration before recreating such a node.
153: ///
154: 
155: ## Restarts
156: 
157: [`containerlab restart`](../../cmd/restart.md) and a `/system reboot` inside RouterOS keep the interface names, MAC addresses, configuration and links: the launcher persists the NIC identity in the container on first boot and does not re-run the bootstrap. A plain `docker restart` keeps the router and its management, but Docker deletes the node's veth links, which stay down until the node is restarted with containerlab or the lab is redeployed.
158: 
159: ## File mounts
160: 
161: For each node containerlab creates in its [lab directory](../conf-artifacts.md):
162: 
163: * `ftpboot/` - mounted to `/ftpboot`, holds `config.auto.rsc`
164: * `chr-launch.sh` - the launcher, mounted read-only to `/chr-launch.sh` and rewritten on every deploy

(End of file - total 164 lines)
</content>

150: // containerlab upgrade ships its launcher to existing labs.
151: func (n *mikrotikCHR) PreDeploy(ctx context.Context, params *clabnodes.PreDeployParams) error {

169: // SaveConfig exports the RouterOS configuration over SSH (scrapligo has no RouterOS
170: // platform, see clabnodes.ExportConfigOverSSH) and writes it as the node's startup config,
171: // without the objects the launcher creates at every boot. Verbose service settings
172: // retain a user override back to main, which compact export omits as a RouterOS default.
173: func (n *mikrotikCHR) SaveConfig(_ context.Context) (*clabnodes.SaveConfigResult, error) {
174: 	exported, err := clabnodes.ExportConfigOverSSH(
175: 		net.JoinHostPort(n.Cfg.LongName, "22"),
176: 		n.Cfg.Credentials.Username,
177: 		n.Cfg.Credentials.Password,
178: 		`/export; :put "# clab-service-defaults"; /ip service export verbose; /snmp export verbose`,
179: 	)
180: 	if err != nil {
181: 		return nil, err
182: 	}
183: 
184: 	return clabnodes.WriteSavedConfig(n.Cfg, n.ConfigDirName, n.StartupCfgFName,
185: 		[]byte(filterLauncherConfig(exported)+"\n"))
186: }
187: 
188: // filterLauncherConfig drops what the launcher configures at every boot from an /export:
189: // every object tagged clab-mgmt (the ether1 management addresses, the mgmt VRF
190: // and its default routes), the ether1 ND entry and CHR's ether1 DHCP client. Imported again
191: // as a startup config, these lines duplicate objects the launcher already created and
192: // RouterOS stops the import at the first one; the management addressing also belongs to
193: // the deployment, not the lab. Continuation lines (an unescaped trailing backslash) are joined
194: // before
195: // matching.
196: func filterLauncherConfig(config string) string {
197: 	var out []string
198: 
199: 	section := ""
200: 	pending := ""
201: 	serviceDefaults := false
202: 	for line := range strings.SplitSeq(strings.ReplaceAll(config, "\r\n", "\n"), "\n") {
203: 		if pending != "" {
204: 			line = pending + "\n" + line
205: 			pending = ""
206: 		}
207: 		if continues(line) {
208: 			pending = line
209: 			continue
210: 		}
211: 
212: 		trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(line)
213: 		if trimmed == "# clab-service-defaults" {
214: 			serviceDefaults = true
215: 			continue
216: 		}
217: 		if strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "/") {
218: 			section = trimmed
219: 		}

221: 		// communities were already exported: adding them twice would fail import.

228: 		out = append(out, line)

231: 		out = append(out, pending)
232: 	}
233: 
234: 	return strings.Join(out, "\n")
235: }

60: You can use [interface names](../topo-def-file.md#interface-naming) in the topology file like they appear in RouterOS: `etherX`, where `X` is the port number.
61: 
62: * `ether2` - first data port
63: * `ether3` - second data port, and so on
64: 
65: /// admonition
66:     type: warning
67: Data ports start at `ether2`: `ether1` is the management interface. Using `ether1` in a topology results in an error.
68: ///
69: 
70: The container interface `ethN` is RouterOS `ether(N+1)`, also when links leave gaps: a link on `eth12` alone still lands on `ether13`, with `ether2` to `ether12` present and unlinked. Interface MTU follows the link MTU, and LLDP frames are forwarded, so `/ip neighbor` shows the peers.
71: 
72: ## Node configuration
73: 
74: -{{ kind_display_name }}- nodes boot with the default CHR configuration plus the credentials, the identity (set to the node name) and the management setup described below.
75: 
76: ### Startup configuration
77: 
78: A RouterOS script (`.rsc`) set with [`startup-config`](../nodes.md#startup-config) is imported once the router is up:
79: 
80: ```yaml
81: name: chr_lab
82: topology:
83:   nodes:
84:     r1:
85:       kind: mikrotik_chr
86:       image: mikrotik/chr:7.24.5
87:       startup-config: r1.rsc
88: ```
89: 
90: The file is copied to the node's lab directory as `ftpboot/config.auto.rsc` and imported over the REST API. RouterOS imports line by line and stops at the first error: in that case the container log carries RouterOS's own reason with the line number, for example
91: 
92: ```
93: chr-launch: startup config import FAILED: Script Error: bad parameter network-type (line 3 column 59); lines before the failing one were applied, the rest were not
94: ```
95: 
96: and the node does not become ready.
97: 
98: ### Saving configuration
99: 
100: [`containerlab save`](../../cmd/save.md) writes each node's `/export` to `ftpboot/config.auto.rsc` in its lab directory. The management objects the launcher creates at every boot (everything tagged `clab-mgmt`, and the `ether1` DHCP client) are left out, so the saved file can be used as the startup config of the next deployment, also one with different management addresses. Service settings include their defaults so an explicit VRF override back to `main` survives the next deployment.
101: 
102: ### Node readiness
103: 
104: The node is ready once RouterOS accepted the credentials and the startup config, reaches its gateway from the management address and, unless the configuration disables SSH, its SSH server answers. An SSH server that does not answer within `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` is logged, and the node is still declared ready, since REST and the console work. The container log then shows
105: 
106: ```
107: chr-launch: RouterOS ready
108: ```
109: 
110: and the kind's default [healthcheck](../nodes.md#healthcheck) reports the container `healthy`, so [`stages`](../nodes.md#stages) with `wait-for` can depend on it. A node whose startup config was rejected never becomes healthy. The default healthcheck's start period follows the launcher's own deadlines (`CHR_INTF_WAIT` + 4 × `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` + 90 s, 1350 s with the defaults), so a slow boot never reports `unhealthy`. A `healthcheck` set in the topology replaces the default one.
111: 
112: ### Resources
113: 
114: The kind reads the official image's own environment variables:
115: 
116: | Variable | Default | Purpose |
117: |----------|---------|---------|
118: | `MEM` | 256 MiB + 8 MiB per data interface and vCPU | VM memory (a QEMU `-m` value, e.g. `1024` or `1G`) |
119: | `CPUS` | `1` | VM vCPUs |
120: | `DISK` | `128M` | minimum disk size (the disk only grows) |
121: | `CHR_INTF_WAIT` | `60` | seconds to wait for the data interfaces containerlab attaches before the VM starts |
122: | `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` | `300` | seconds to wait for RouterOS to answer, for the VRF handoff, for the startup config import, and for SSH before the node is declared ready |
123: 
124: ```yaml
125: r1:
126:   kind: mikrotik_chr
127:   image: mikrotik/chr:7.24.5
128:   env:
129:     MEM: 1024
130:     CPUS: 2
131: ```
132: 
133: KVM is used when `/dev/kvm` is available. Without it the image's QEMU runs under TCG emulation: the node works, but boots several times slower.
134: 
135: ## Management connectivity
136: 
137: Management is transparent: the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and gateways containerlab gives the node's `eth0` are configured on RouterOS `ether1`, and the container's `eth0` is bridged to the VM's `ether1`. The address in the topology table is the one in the RouterOS configuration.
138: 
139: The image ships busybox only (no `tc`), so where vrnetlab's [transparent management](../vrnetlab.md#management-interface) redirects with tc-mirred, this kind uses a Linux bridge. The container itself has no address on the management network; it reaches RouterOS for bootstrap over IPv6 link-local on that bridge.
140: 
141: The launcher places `ether1` in a native `mgmt` VRF before `main`. RouterOS creates its routing table and connected routes; the launcher adds IPv4 and IPv6 defaults that resolve their gateways in `mgmt`. No source-policy rules or route leaks are added. Data interfaces remain in `main`, so a lab default route does not take management replies away from `ether1`. CHR's `ether1` DHCP client is disabled.
142: 
143: On first boot, one RouterOS background job creates the VRF and binds SSH, HTTP/HTTPS (including REST), API/API-SSL, Winbox, Telnet and SNMP to it. Their enabled/disabled state is preserved. The launcher waits for the native routing table and service bindings before configuring management addressing, joining the external management bridge and fetching the startup config through `mgmt`. On restart, startup-config service overrides are preserved. The launcher uses HTTP/REST with the topology credentials during container startup. SSH in `mgmt` provides user login access and is also used by `containerlab save`. Credential setup, service ports and access controls are unchanged.
144: 
145: A service's VRF binding also changes where it can be reached: these services no longer listen through data interfaces in `main` unless the startup config changes their binding. RouterOS FTP does not support VRF binding and is unavailable through the management VRF. Other router-originated services, such as DNS, NTP and logging, need their own VRF-aware configuration to use management egress. RouterOS applies its VRF interface matching to firewall rules; see the [RouterOS VRF documentation](https://manual.mikrotik.com/docs/user-guides/routing-and-networking-protocols/vrf/).
146: 
147: VRF membership does not disable Layer 2 neighbor discovery. LLDP, CDP and MNDP follow `/ip neighbor discovery-settings`; use an explicit interface list excluding `ether1` when management discovery is unwanted.
148: 
149: RouterOS's router advertisements on `ether1` carry a zero router lifetime, so no host on the management network takes the router as its IPv6 default gateway. The container joins the management network only once this is in place. Management objects carry the comment `clab-mgmt` and are re-applied at boot when the container's addressing changed.

(Showing lines 60-149 of 164. Use offset=150 to continue.)

59:  ## Management connectivity
60:  
61: -Management is transparent: the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and gateways containerlab gives the node's `eth0` are configured on RouterOS `ether1`, and the container's `eth0` is bridged to the VM's `ether1`. The router is the node's management address: SSH, the REST API, Winbox, SNMP and every other service answer on it, LLDP/MNDP work on the management network, and the address in the topology table is the one in the RouterOS configuration.
62: +Management is transparent: the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and gateways containerlab gives the node's `eth0` are configured on RouterOS `ether1`, and the container's `eth0` is bridged to the VM's `ether1`. The address in the topology table is the one in the RouterOS configuration.
63:  
64:  The image ships busybox only (no `tc`), so where vrnetlab's [transparent management](../vrnetlab.md#management-interface) redirects with tc-mirred, this kind uses a Linux bridge. The container itself has no address on the management network; it reaches RouterOS for bootstrap over IPv6 link-local on that bridge.
65:  
66: -The management return path lives in its own routing table, `mgmt`, selected by routing rules for the management addresses, and CHR's `ether1` DHCP client is disabled. A default route in the lab configuration, a PPPoE client's default route or a dual-WAN setup in `main` therefore does not cut SSH or REST access to the node. RouterOS's router advertisements on `ether1` carry a zero router lifetime, so no host on the management network takes the router as its IPv6 default gateway; the container joins the management network only once this is in place. The objects carry the comment `clab-mgmt` and are re-applied at boot when the container's addressing changed.
67: +The launcher places `ether1` in a native `mgmt` VRF before `main`. RouterOS creates its routing table and connected routes; the launcher adds IPv4 and IPv6 defaults that resolve their gateways in `mgmt`. No source-policy rules or route leaks are added. Data interfaces remain in `main`, so a lab default route does not take management replies away from `ether1`. CHR's `ether1` DHCP client is disabled.
68: +
69: +On first boot, one RouterOS background job creates the VRF and binds SSH, HTTP/HTTPS (including REST), API/API-SSL, Winbox, Telnet and SNMP to it. Their enabled/disabled state is preserved. The launcher waits for the native routing table and service bindings before configuring management addressing, joining the external management bridge and fetching the startup config through `mgmt`. On restart, startup-config service overrides are preserved. The launcher uses HTTP/REST with the topology credentials during container startup. SSH in `mgmt` provides user login access and is also used by `containerlab save`. Credential setup, service ports and access controls are unchanged.
70: +
71: +A service's VRF binding also changes where it can be reached: these services no longer listen through data interfaces in `main` unless the startup config changes their binding. RouterOS FTP does not support VRF binding and is unavailable through the management VRF. Other router-originated services, such as DNS, NTP and logging, need their own VRF-aware configuration to use management egress. RouterOS applies its VRF interface matching to firewall rules; see the [RouterOS VRF documentation](https://manual.mikrotik.com/docs/user-guides/routing-and-networking-protocols/vrf/).
72: +
73: +VRF membership does not disable Layer 2 neighbor discovery. LLDP, CDP and MNDP follow `/ip neighbor discovery-settings`; use an explicit interface list excluding `ether1` when management discovery is unwanted.
74: +
75: +RouterOS's router advertisements on `ether1` carry a zero router lifetime, so no host on the management network takes the router as its IPv6 default gateway. The container joins the management network only once this is in place. Management objects carry the comment `clab-mgmt` and are re-applied at boot when the container's addressing changed.

78: -Do not remove or change the `clab-mgmt` objects or the `mgmt` routing table: management of the node depends on them.
79: +Do not remove or change the `clab-mgmt` objects or the `mgmt` VRF: management of the node depends on them. This setup requires a fresh node container; it does not migrate a running node that uses the previous policy-only `mgmt` table. Export the user configuration before recreating such a node.
80:  ///

82:  ## Restarts
83:  
84:  [`containerlab restart`](../../cmd/restart.md) and a `/system reboot` inside RouterOS keep the interface names, MAC addresses, configuration and links: the launcher persists the NIC identity in the container on first boot and does not re-run the bootstrap. A plain `docker restart` keeps the router and its management, but Docker deletes the node's veth links, which stay down until the node is restarted with containerlab or the lab is redeployed.

Service settings include their defaults so an explicit VRF override back to `main` survives the next deployment.\n \n ### Node readiness\n \n The node is ready once RouterOS accepted the credentials and the startup config, reaches its gateway from the management address and, unless the configuration disables SSH, its SSH server answers. An SSH server that does not answer within `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` is logged, and the node is still declared ready, since REST and the console work. The container log then shows\n \n ```\n chr-launch: RouterOS ready\n ```\n \n-and the kind's default [healthcheck](../nodes.md#healthcheck) reports the container `healthy`, so [`stages`](../nodes.md#stages) with `wait-for` can depend on it. A node whose startup config was rejected never becomes healthy. The default healthcheck's start period follows the launcher's own deadlines (`CHR_INTF_WAIT` + 3 × `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` + 90 s, 1050 s with the defaults), so a slow boot never reports `unhealthy`. ## Code Review: mikrotik CHR — policy-routing `mgmt` table → native `mgmt` VRF

### Summary

The PR replaces the CHR launcher's source-policy routing rules and static `mgmt` routing table with a native RouterOS VRF that binds `ether1` and all management services, and extends `containerlab save` with a verbose service/SNMP tail so a user's VRF override back to `main` survives the save/deploy round trip. The diff spans four files: the launcher (`chr-launch.sh`), the Go node (`mikrotik_chr.go`), its tests, and the kind documentation.

The design is coherent and the documentation matches the implementation closely (service list, FTP exclusion, restart semantics, the `CHR_INTF_WAIT` + 4 × `CHR_BOOT_WAIT` + 90 s start-period formula, and the explicit "requires a fresh container" migration warning for pre-VRF nodes). I verified the call graph end to end: `filterLauncherConfig` and `ExportConfigOverSSH` have no other callers, `ipcalc` and `routing/rule` handling were removed consistently, and the unchanged robot e2e suite (`tests/16-mikrotik-chr/01-chr.robot`) exercises deploy-with-startup-config, custom credentials, rejected import, and `save`, which catches most RouterOS API semantic mistakes in CI.

Two findings, both about the save-filter logic and its tests:

| Priority | Count | Summary |
|----------|-------|---------|
| P0 | 0 | — |
| P1 | 0 | — |
| P2 | 0 | — |
| P3 | 1 | Coupled, untested marker between `SaveConfig` and `filterLauncherConfig` |
| P4 | 1 | Stale test fixture no longer matches launcher output; new filter branch untested |

### Finding details

#### P3 — `# clab-service-defaults` marker is a duplicated, untested coupling between `SaveConfig` and `filterLauncherConfig`

Location: [`nodes/mikrotik_chr/mikrotik_chr.go` L178, L213–L224](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/blob/77d24e9da2cf391be6f422e382af08feb98cc581/nodes/mikrotik_chr/mikrotik_chr.go#L178-L224)

Problem: the marker `# clab-service-defaults` exists as two independent string literals in the same file — once inside the SSH command built in `SaveConfig` (line 178: `` `/export; :put "# clab-service-defaults"; /ip service export verbose; /snmp export verbose` ``) and once as the comparison value in `filterLauncherConfig` (line 213). The new `serviceDefaults` branch also hard-codes the allow-list `"/ip service"` and `"/snmp"`, which must stay in lockstep with the commands appended after the `:put`. A grep of the whole tree confirms no test references this marker: the new branch has zero unit-test coverage (the only filter tests are `TestFilterLauncherConfig`, `TestFilterLauncherConfigContinuationLines`, and `TestFilterLauncherConfigEscapedBackslash`, none of which include the tail).

Trigger: any future edit of one side of this coupling. Dropping or renaming `:put "# clab-service-defaults"` leaves the verbose tail fully included (benign duplication), but adding a new verbose section to the command — say `/ip firewall export verbose` — without updating the allow-list silently drops that whole section from the saved file, because the branch discards every post-marker section that is not `/ip service` or `/snmp`.

Impact: `containerlab save` would silently produce an incomplete `config.auto.rsc`, and the documented behavior that "an explicit VRF override back to `main` survives the next deployment" would regress without any failing check. This is exactly the kind of latent one-token breakage the duplicated magic string plus missing test makes cheap to introduce.

Suggestion: define a single exported/unexported constant (e.g. `serviceDefaultsMarker = "# clab-service-defaults"`) used in both the command and the filter, and add one table-driven case to `TestFilterLauncherConfig` covering the marker plus a verbose tail with `/ip service` and `/snmp` sections and a dropped non-service section.

#### P4 — `exportedConfig` fixture models the removed policy-table launcher; the changed filter path is exercised only against stale output

Location: [`nodes/mikrotik_chr/mikrotik_chr_test.go` L201–L241](https://github.com/srl-labs/containerlab/blob/77d24e9da2cf391be6f422e382af08feb98cc581/nodes/mikrotik_chr/mikrotik_chr_test.go#L201-L241)

Problem: the fixture is commented as "a verbatim RouterOS 7.24.5 /export of a node this kind deployed", but this PR changed what the kind deploys: the fixture contains `/routing table add comment=clab-mgmt fib name=mgmt` and `/routing rule` lines that the VRF launcher no longer creates, and lacks the `/ip vrf add name=mgmt interfaces=ether1 comment=clab-mgmt` object and the `/ip service` / `/snmp` sections with `vrf=mgmt` that a real export now contains. `TestFilterLauncherConfig` still passes because the clab-mgmt comment matching is unchanged, but the kept-list assertion `"/routing table"` (line 266) now asserts against an artifact the kind will no longer produce.

Trigger: every run of the unit tests after this PR.

Impact: no incorrect behavior today, but the suite validates the filter against a configuration shape the launcher no longer emits, and the new post-marker filtering path (the most subtle logic in the diff) runs only against pre-PR-shaped input. This compounds finding 1.

Suggestion: refresh `exportedConfig` to a VRF-world export (including the `/ip vrf` line with `comment=clab-mgmt`, service lines carrying `vrf=mgmt`, and a marker plus verbose tail) — this simultaneously closes finding 1's coverage gap and makes the fixture description true again.

### Coverage notes

- This was a source-only review; no tests were executed and no RouterOS instance was available. Nothing in this review should be read as a CI run result.
- RouterOS API semantics cannot be confirmed from the snapshot: the `dynamic=false` filter on `/rest/ip/service`, the round-trip of `gateway=$G4@$MGMT_TABLE` in the `mgmt_in_place` query, the `vrf` parameter on `/rest/ping`, and the `LL%ether1@$MGMT_TABLE` suffix in the `tool/fetch` address. Each of these fails visibly if wrong (a node that never becomes ready, or a logged "gateway does not answer" warning), and the unchanged e2e suite exercises all of them against RouterOS 7.24.5 in CI; the CI result is the authoritative check for these items.
- Edge-case behavior change, noted for awareness only: when both management addresses are empty, the new final `mgmt_in_place || mgmt_fail "management addressing or routes not applied"` kills the container where the base only logged and continued. This is practically unreachable (containerlab always assigns management addressing) and failing loudly on a management-less node is defensible, but the message would be misleading if it ever fired.
- Migration and compatibility were verified against the docs: pre-VRF nodes are blocked on restart by the `mgmt_fail` guard with an actionable message, the docs warning explicitly requires a fresh container with export-before-recreate, and the saved-config round trip (launcher binds services before import, tail preserves overrides) is consistent.
- No topology schema or CLI API changes are involved, so no `clab.schema.json` review was needed. Docs changes are limited to `mikrotik_chr.md` and are consistent with the implementation.
